subtype: Approach: root-cause thinking about how data was shared so freely [Thinking]
passage:
Rajni, you asked what changed my habits, and it wasn't the breach itself. It was the question I asked afterwards: why did six different services already hold my name, my number and my birthday? Nobody forced me. I just typed it all in, every time, because the form had boxes.

So I traced it back. Most of those boxes were optional. I never read the permission screens either, I just pressed accept. That was the real root of it.

Now I give the minimum, and I skip optional fields. I made a separate email address only for sign-ups. And I read what an app asks for before saying yes, even if it takes a minute. I'm Tarun, and I've deleted four accounts I didn't need.

qa.q: What did Tarun make for sign-ups?
qa.a: A separate email address only for sign-ups.

qa.q: What might Tarun have been feeling when tracing the six services back to habit?
qa.a: Tarun was probably uneasy and a little embarrassed at having shared so freely, since habit and not any need was the real cause.

qa.q: What could Tarun do next to keep the new habit from slipping, and why?
qa.a: Tarun could check once a season which accounts still hold personal details and remove the ones not used, because habits need a regular reminder.

qa.q: How might Rajni, who asked the question, see Tarun's answer?
qa.a: Rajni may notice that Tarun blames the habit instead of the breach, which makes the answer useful to anyone who hears it.

grounding: Asking why so many services held the same details, the person decides to give minimum data, use a separate sign-up email and read permissions.

subtype: Approach: alert friends and family to expect phishing [Action]
passage:
The leak had taken Jamal's contact list, and he knew his relatives in three countries would be next. On Saturday morning in Melbourne, before his tea went cold, he wrote in the family group: "My contacts were in a data leak. If a message comes from me or anyone asking for money, a code or a quick favour, please don't reply. Ring me instead."

Then he phoned his grandmother, who did not use the group, and read it to her slowly. He asked her to tell Aunty Sofia's household the same.

By noon his cousin Tuan wrote back, "Got a weird message from 'you' an hour ago. Ignored it. Good thing you warned us." Jamal felt his shoulders drop.

qa.q: Who did Jamal phone after posting in the family group?
qa.a: His grandmother, who did not use the group.

qa.q: What was Jamal feeling when Tuan's reply arrived?
qa.a: Jamal felt relieved, shown by his shoulders dropping when he learned the warning had come in time.

qa.q: What else could Jamal do for relatives who might still fall for a message, and why?
qa.a: Jamal could agree on a family code word to check that a request is really from him, because a shared check makes fake requests easy to spot.

qa.q: How might Tuan see the suspicious message once Jamal's warning arrived?
qa.a: Tuan probably felt confident to ignore it, since the warning made the strange message obviously suspect instead of confusing.

grounding: Because contact lists were part of the leak, the person tells relatives to ignore suspicious messages asking for money or codes.

subtype: Approach: assume nothing is at risk because nothing was stolen [Pitfall]
passage:
When the news said Omar's fitness app had leaked email addresses, he shrugged. "Only my email. No password, no card. Who cares?" His sister Mina, visiting from Toronto, raised an eyebrow, but Omar had already returned to the video game.

Three months later an email arrived with his full name, his gym's name and a photo taken from his public profile. It said his membership was overdue and asked him to pay a small fee through a link. It looked so personal that he clicked, and only stopped at the payment page when Mina looked over his shoulder and said, "How would they know all that?" The fee was fake, and Omar spent the evening changing passwords and feeling foolish about what small pieces add up to.

qa.q: What did Omar say when he learned about the leak?
qa.a: Omar said it was only his email, with no password or card, and asked who cared.

qa.q: How did Omar feel when Mina stopped him at the payment page?
qa.a: Omar felt foolish and shaken, realising he had nearly been fooled by a message that seemed personal.

qa.q: What could Omar do to protect himself against such messages in future, and why?
qa.a: Omar could check any unexpected fee by going to the gym directly, because a real membership issue can be confirmed without using the link.

qa.q: How does Mina see Omar's first shrug compared with what happened later?
qa.a: Mina had raised an eyebrow because a leaked address may join other details, so the later personal email showed her doubt was fair.

grounding: The person assumes an email-only leak is harmless, but later the address combined with other data enables a targeted scam.

subtype: Approach: decide which tasks the tool should and should not do [Thinking]
passage:
Day 1. Vasudha, in her final year, wrote three lines in her project notebook and taped them above her desk. AI may explain a concept I don't follow. AI may check my grammar. AI may not write my analysis. She thought: if I decide what the tool is for before I open it, I won't drift.

Day 4. At one in the morning, tired, she opened the tool and felt the pull to ask it for the whole results section. She read the taped lines, closed the window, and asked it instead to explain what a confidence interval means. Then she wrote the paragraph herself.

Day 9. Her classmate Pranav asked, "Can I see your prompt for the analysis?" Vasudha laughed. "I don't have one. I have a rule." She showed him the paper on the wall.

qa.q: Where did Vasudha put her three rules?
qa.a: She taped them above her desk.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling at one in the morning when she felt the pull to ask for the results section?
qa.a: Vasudha was tired and tempted, but her reading the rules and closing the window shows a determination to keep the work her own.

qa.q: What could Vasudha do if she was ever unsure whether a request fits her rules, and why?
qa.a: Vasudha could ask whether the tool would be doing the thinking or helping her understand, because the purpose of the request decides whether it belongs.

qa.q: How might Pranav see Vasudha's rule?
qa.a: Pranav may find it a surprisingly simple answer, and could be prompted to think about what he wants the tool to do for him.

grounding: A final-year student sets a rule that AI may explain and check grammar but not write the analysis, choosing the purpose first.

subtype: Approach: verify AI outputs against reliable sources [Action]
passage:
Selin pasted a summary of a research paper into her notes, and it read beautifully: one clear claim, a percentage, and two citations. Before using it in her seminar talk, she made a small list. One: find the paper. Two: read the abstract and the results table. Three: look for the percentage. Four: search for each citation.

From her flat in Istanbul, she opened the original on her laptop. The percentage was close but not the same, and the paper said "in a small sample," which the summary had dropped. One of the citations did not exist at all.

She corrected the number, added the caveat, and sent her friend Sofia a quick message: "Glad I checked. Never trusting a tidy summary again."

qa.q: How many citations did the summary give, and how many turned out not to exist?
qa.a: The summary gave two citations, and one of them did not exist at all.

qa.q: What was Selin feeling when she saw the citation did not exist?
qa.a: Selin was surprised and relieved, since the check had caught an error before it reached her talk.

qa.q: What could Selin do next time she wants a quick overview, and why?
qa.a: Selin could use the summary only as a map and read the original paper's abstract and results herself, because a tidy summary can be wrong while still sounding sure.

qa.q: How might Sofia see Selin's message?
qa.a: Sofia may feel the lesson is useful for Sofia's own work and admire the care Selin took before speaking to the seminar.

grounding: Before using an AI summary, the person checks the claims and citations against the original paper.

subtype: Approach: paste the assignment and submit the result [Pitfall]
passage:
"Farida, sit down. Read this paragraph aloud for me."

"Professor Mridul, I—"

"Please."

"'The novel critiques colonial railway policy in the seventh chapter.'"

"There is no railway in the seventh chapter, and the book has no colonial chapter at all. Also, this quote does not appear anywhere in the text."

Farida's face went hot. "I ran out of time. I put the question into a tool and submitted what it gave me."

"The college rules say your submission must be your own work. You will need to write it again, with a note to the committee. You'll also lose the marks for this one."

"I know. I'm sorry. I didn't learn anything, did I?"

"Not from that one."

qa.q: What did the professor say was missing from the seventh chapter?
qa.a: There is no railway in the seventh chapter.

qa.q: What is Farida feeling as Farida's face goes hot?
qa.a: Farida feels embarrassed and regretful, having taken a shortcut under time pressure that has now cost marks.

qa.q: What could Farida do next time when short of time, and why?
qa.a: Farida could ask the professor for a short extension or submit a smaller honest draft, because an honest partial attempt teaches more than a polished copy.

qa.q: How might Professor Mridul see the submitted essay?
qa.a: Professor Mridul sees work with invented quotes that does not show what Farida understands, and is bound by the rules on originality.

grounding: Pressed for time, a student submits an AI-written essay unchanged, and the errors, policy breach and lack of learning cost more later.

subtype: Approach: read the institution and employer AI policy first [Action]
passage:
Honestly, what stopped me was a guideline I almost skipped, so I'm glad I read it. I'm Noor, and last spring I was told to summarise a forty-page client contract. The quickest way was to paste it into a chatbot on the internet. My hand was already on the mouse.

But something nagged me, so I opened the company's AI guideline first. It said clearly that client documents must never go into public services, and that only approved tools were allowed. I then asked my manager Gargi which tool I could use. She smiled and pointed me to the internal one. It was slower, and I read a lot more myself. But the client's name never left our systems, and I slept fine.

qa.q: How many pages was the client contract?
qa.a: Forty pages.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when something nagged before pasting the contract?
qa.a: Noor felt uneasy and cautious, sensing a possible mistake even with a hand already on the mouse.

qa.q: What could Noor do if the internal tool could not handle the contract, and why?
qa.a: Noor could tell Gargi and ask for another approved way to get help, because the rule protects the client and a workaround would break it.

qa.q: How might Gargi see Noor's question about approved tools?
qa.a: Gargi likely felt pleased, seeing a team member who checks the rules first and can be trusted with client material.

grounding: The employee checks the company AI guideline before pasting client documents into a public chatbot and asks the manager about approved tools.

subtype: Approach: use the tool as a tutor with own attempt first [Thinking]
passage:
Nandini's laptop fan whirred in the small computer lab of the polytechnic in Kasba. Her program to sort marks kept crashing on line twelve. She wanted to ask the tool for the finished code, but stopped: if I get it now, I won't know why it broke.

So she stared at the error for ten minutes, tried changing the loop twice, and failed. Only then did she paste the error and her attempt and ask, "Explain what this message means. Don't write the solution." The tool said she was mixing text and numbers. "Now ask me three questions about that so I know I've got it," she typed.

Gopika, at the next desk, saw her fix it and asked, "How?" Nandini grinned. "I tried first, then it taught me."

qa.q: On which line did Nandini's program keep crashing?
qa.a: On line twelve.

qa.q: Why did Nandini decide to stare at the error before asking the tool?
qa.a: Nandini feared that receiving finished code would leave her not knowing why it broke, so she wanted to keep her own thinking active.

qa.q: What could Nandini do if the tool's explanation still confused her, and why?
qa.a: Nandini could ask Gopika at the next desk to walk through the error with her, because a person can see what she already understands.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel after seeing Nandini fix the crash?
qa.a: Gopika may feel curious and a little encouraged, wanting to try the same try-first method on Gopika's own program.

grounding: The student attempts a coding problem first, then asks the tool to explain the error and quiz her on the concept.

subtype: Approach: trust the output because it sounds fluent [Pitfall]
passage:
Note on Aditi's quarterly report, written by Reena, team manager.

On Tuesday I was checking Aditi's draft before it went to the client and noticed a growth figure that looked too neat. I searched for its source and found nothing. When I asked, Aditi said the tool had produced it and it sounded right, so she added it without checking.

The number was invented. Had it gone out, we would have lost credibility with the client.

I sat with Aditi and we removed the figure, replaced it with the real number from the records, and re-sent the draft. She was upset and apologised twice. I told her that fluent writing is not proof of accuracy, and we agreed that every figure gets a source line before I see it.

qa.q: On which day did Reena notice the figure?
qa.a: On Tuesday.

qa.q: What might Aditi have been feeling when she apologised twice?
qa.a: Aditi was upset and embarrassed, realising the invented number could have harmed the client's trust.

qa.q: What could Aditi do to catch such problems herself, and why?
qa.a: Aditi could add a source line for every figure and check each against the records before sharing, because a fluent answer proves nothing about accuracy.

qa.q: What would have changed for the client if the figure had gone out?
qa.a: The client would have trusted a number that was not real, and the team would have lost credibility once it was discovered.

grounding: A young analyst uses a tool-generated figure without checking, and the manager finds the number invented, mistaking fluency for accuracy.

subtype: Approach: add disclosure and keep a record of use [Revision]
passage:
"Thomas, before you go. Which parts of this essay did you write yourself?"

"Most of it, Professor Sonali. I used the tool for the outline and to smooth two paragraphs."

"And where does it say that?"

"It doesn't." He shifted in his chair. "I didn't think it mattered."

"It matters because I can't tell which ideas are yours."

Thomas nodded slowly. "Okay. I'll keep a note from now on."

A week later he stood at her door again with a printout. "There's a line at the end this time: 'Outline suggested by an AI tool; paragraphs two and five edited with it.' And I've saved the prompts."

Sonali smiled. "Now I know exactly what is yours."

qa.q: What did Thomas add at the end of the essay?
qa.a: A line saying the outline was suggested by an AI tool and that paragraphs two and five were edited with it.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when Sonali asked where his essay said the tool was used?
qa.a: Thomas felt awkward and a little caught out, shown by shifting in his chair and admitting he had not thought it mattered.

qa.q: What could Thomas do next if he is unsure whether a use of the tool needs mentioning, and why?
qa.a: Thomas could ask Professor Sonali or check the course rules, because an early question is safer than a surprise later.

qa.q: How might Sonali see the extra line in Thomas's essay?
qa.a: Sonali sees an honest record that lets her tell which ideas are Thomas's own, and it rebuilds her trust.

grounding: After a professor's question, the student notes where AI helped and adds an acknowledgment, which clarifies what is their own work.
